facts.text: A 2021 study of over 6,000 people found that, adjusted for body size, daily energy use stays steady from about 20 to 60.
India's dietary guidelines (ICMR-NIN, 2024) estimate that about 56% of the country's disease burden is linked to unhealthy diets.
Folate before and in early pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube defects. Dals, leafy greens and fortified foods help.
ICMR-NIN's model plate fills about half with vegetables and fruit; grains, pulses, nuts and dairy share the rest.
From around 30, muscle slowly declines with age, by roughly 3–8% a decade without training against it.
The WHO suggests under 5 g of salt a day, about a teaspoon. Indian adults average around 8 g, much of it from pickles, namkeen and restaurant food.
Many Indians gain fat around the waist first, even at a normal BMI. This 'thin-fat' pattern is linked to diabetes risk.
One tablespoon of pickle can carry 1–2 g of salt, a third of a day's limit.
ICMR-INDIAB (2023) found about 11% of Indian adults have diabetes and another 15% prediabetes.
A tablespoon of oil or ghee is about 120 kcal. A two-spoon tadka adds as much energy as two or three rotis.
ICMR-NIN sets women's iron need at about 29 mg a day, over 50% more than men's 19 mg.
A medium phulka from about 30 g of atta is roughly 100 kcal. A teaspoon of ghee on top adds about 45 more.
In your thirties and forties, watching your waist can say more about metabolic risk than the scale.
Cereals run short of lysine and pulses short of methionine. Together, as dal-chawal or rajma-chawal, they make a more complete protein.
At 156–160 cm, the healthy weight range used for Indian adults (BMI 18.5–22.9) is about 45–59 kg.
Soaking and sprouting pulses cuts phytates, which helps your body absorb more of their iron and zinc.
A waist under half your height is a simple heart-health target: at 156–160 cm, that's under about 78–80 cm.
Cooking in an iron kadhai or tawa can add iron to food, especially sour dishes made with tomato or tamarind.
At 51–55 kg, ICMR-NIN's minimum is about 42–46 g of protein a day. If you train, 1.2–1.6 g per kg puts it at about 61–88 g.
Vitamin C breaks down with heat. Squeeze lemon on dal or sabzi after cooking, not while it simmers.
At 51–55 kg, a 5 km run burns roughly 255–275 kcal, about the same as a samosa.
Tannins in tea and coffee reduce the iron you absorb from a meal. Have chai an hour before or after eating.
At 51–55 kg, walking off one samosa (about 260 kcal) takes roughly 6.3–6.8 km at a brisk pace.
Gram for gram, ragi has roughly three times the calcium of milk.
A common rule of thumb is 30–35 mL of fluid per kg a day: about 1.5–1.9 litres at 51–55 kg, more in heat or training.
Gram for gram, amla carries several times the vitamin C of an orange.
Vegetarians get B12 mainly from milk, curd and paneer, and many still run low. It's worth testing.
Juice loses most of the fruit's fibre, so a glass fills you up far less than the fruit it took to make.
Iron from plants is absorbed less than iron from meat, so pairing it with vitamin C matters more for vegetarians.
The WHO advises keeping free sugars under 10% of daily energy, ideally under 5%: about 25 g, or six teaspoons, for most adults.
Paneer is protein-dense: about 18 g per 100 g, with calcium as a bonus.
Two teaspoons of sugar a cup adds up: three cups a day is around 25–30 g of sugar, already at the WHO's ideal limit.
Soy chunks are among the richest plant proteins: about 50 g per 100 g, dry.
A 300 mL bottle of cola has around 30 g of sugar, more than the WHO's ideal limit for a whole day.
Adults need about 25–30 g of fibre a day. A katori of rajma or chana gives roughly 6–9 g of it.
Studies suggest muscles use protein better when it's spread across meals than when most of it comes at dinner.
Fullness signals take time to reach your brain. Eating slowly gives them a chance to arrive before second helpings do.
In sleep studies, short nights raised the hunger hormone ghrelin and lowered leptin, which signals fullness.
Homemade dahi carries live lactic acid bacteria, and fermentation makes its lactose easier for many people to digest.
Jowar, bajra and ragi carry more fibre than polished rice, so they digest more slowly.
Reheating frying oil again and again creates harmful compounds. ICMR-NIN's guidelines advise against reusing it.
About a fifth of the water you take in comes from food: dal, sabzi, curd and fruit all count.
A protein-rich breakfast, like eggs, besan chilla or paneer, tends to keep you fuller through the morning than one of only carbs.
In large studies, a small handful of nuts most days, about 30 g, is linked with lower heart-disease risk.
Few foods carry much vitamin D. Sunlight is the main source; fortified milk, egg yolks and fatty fish add a little.
Calcium competes with iron for absorption. If you take an iron tablet, keep it apart from milk and curd.
Cut fruit loses vitamin C to air and light as it sits. Eat it soon after cutting.
In several studies, people served on bigger plates ate more. A smaller thali can quietly mean a smaller portion.
Alcohol has 7 kcal per gram, nearly as much as fat. A 60 mL peg of whisky is about 130 kcal before any mixer.
In the standard formula for resting energy, each centimetre of height adds about 6 kcal a day.
Muscle uses more energy at rest than fat does, which is one reason strength training helps keep weight steady.
